exploreAction.instruction: Read how the theory shaped colonial policy, then trace how the restrictions of mercantilism helped provoke colonial revolts.

name: The Feudal System of Japan (12th-19th century)
teaser: Japan's samurai class, sworn to daimyo lords, governed under a system of hereditary military rule with the emperor as figurehead. The shogun — 'barbarian-subduing generalissimo' — held real power, and the code of bushido governed warrior conduct. The system ended with the Meiji Restoration of 1868.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the shogunate rose from the Gempei War, then trace the samurai code and the system's end in the Meiji reforms.

name: The Siege of Troy (c. 1200 BCE?)
teaser: The ten-year siege of Troy, as told by Homer, ended not with assault but with a trick: Greeks hidden inside a wooden horse, opened the city's gates at night. Whether the Trojan War happened, and whether there was a real horse, remains archaeology's greatest debate. The tale defined Greek identity and literature for three thousand years.

exploreAction.instruction: Read Homer's account of the war's end, then weigh the archaeological evidence from Hisarlik for a real Trojan conflict.

name: The Siege of Masada (73-74 CE)
teaser: Roman legions built a ramp to breach the desert fortress where Jewish rebels had held out after the fall of Jerusalem. Rather than surrender, the defenders — according to Josephus — chose mass suicide, 960 people. Masada became a symbol of Jewish resistance, and its excavation remains a pilgrimage site.
byline: The Roman legions and the Jewish rebels

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the siege ramp was built and how the fortress fell, then consider how the story has been used and debated in modern Israel.

name: The Siege of Leningrad (1941-1944)
teaser: The German army surrounded Leningrad for 872 days, and the city starved: over a million civilians died, many of them eating bread made mostly of sawdust. The 'Road of Life' across the frozen Lake Ladoga supplied a trickle of food. The city never surrendered — a defiance that made it a Soviet symbol of endurance.
byline: The German army vs. the people of Leningrad

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the city survived the blockade, then examine the diary of Tanya Savicheva, one of the siege's most famous records.

name: The Siege of Sarajevo (1992-1996)
teaser: The longest siege of a capital city in modern history lasted nearly four years, as Bosnian Serb forces surrounded Sarajevo during the Bosnian War. Snipers and shelling killed over 11,000 civilians, including the 'bread line massacre.' The city's residents dug tunnels and held on as the world watched. The siege ended with the Dayton Agreement in 1995.
byline: The Bosnian Serb forces and the defenders of Sarajevo

exploreAction.instruction: Read how daily life continued under fire, then examine the siege's toll and the war crimes trials that followed.

name: The Trial of Socrates (399 BCE)
teaser: Accused of impiety and corrupting the youth of Athens, Socrates defended himself with the questions that had made him famous — and was convicted by a narrow margin. He refused to escape, drank the hemlock, and died arguing about the soul. Plato turned his teacher's death into the founding story of Western philosophy.

exploreAction.instruction: Read Plato's account of the Apology, then consider why Athens killed its gadfly and why Socrates refused to flee.

name: The Trial of Galileo (1633)
teaser: For defending the Copernican idea that the Earth moves around the Sun, Galileo was tried by the Inquisition and forced to recant. Under threat of torture, he muttered that the Earth nonetheless moves — legend says 'eppur si muove.' He spent his last years under house arrest, still writing science. The church formally acknowledged its error in 1992.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the telescope's discoveries alarmed the church, then trace the long road from condemnation to the 1992 acknowledgement.

name: The Trial of Oscar Wilde (1895)
teaser: The era's most famous playwright sued the Marquess of Queensberry for libel over an insulting card — and the case collapsed into Wilde's own trial for 'gross indecency.' Convicted, Wilde served two years of hard labor and died in exile in Paris at 46. His trials made him a martyr for art and a symbol of the Victorian double standard.
byline: Oscar Wilde and the Victorian legal system

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Wilde's libel suit backfired, then consider how the trials revealed Victorian society's attitudes toward art and sexuality.

name: The Industrial Revolution in Japan (1870s-1900s)
teaser: The Meiji government, determined to catch the West, built railways, telegraphs, and factories with state money and imported expertise. Japan's first industrialists — the zaibatsu — grew into conglomerates like Mitsubishi and Sumitomo. Within a generation, Japan produced its own steel, ships, and weapons — and its own empire.
byline: The Meiji government and the zaibatsu

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the state directed industrialization, then trace how the zaibatsu conglomerates came to dominate the economy.

name: The Iranian Revolution (1979)
teaser: Mass protests against the Shah's secular, Western-backed monarchy toppled a dynasty in months and brought Ayatollah Khomeini to power from exile. The revolution replaced the Pahlavi monarchy with an Islamic Republic, and its shockwaves — the hostage crisis, the Iran-Iraq war — reshaped the Middle East. It remains the defining event of modern Iran.
byline: Ayatollah Khomeini and the Iranian people

exploreAction.instruction: Read how decades of discontent united around Khomeini, then trace the revolution's consolidation and its regional consequences.

name: James Cook's Pacific Voyages (1768-1779)
teaser: Captain Cook charted the Pacific more completely than anyone before him, mapping New Zealand, the east coast of Australia, and Hawaii, and crossing the Antarctic Circle. He was the first to largely defeat scurvy by feeding his crews citrus. He was killed in Hawaii in 1779 during a misunderstanding with islanders.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Cook's mapping opened the Pacific to Europe, then consider the encounters with Pacific peoples and how his voyages changed them.

name: The Race to the South Pole (1911-1912)
teaser: Roald Amundsen's Norwegian team reached the South Pole on December 14, 1911, beating Robert Falcon Scott's British team by a month. Amundsen used dogs and skis; Scott used ponies and man-hauling and died with his party on the return. The race became a parable of preparation versus pluck.

exploreAction.targetName: the race to the South Pole
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Amundsen's planning won the race, then examine Scott's tragic return and the century of debate over his decisions.

name: The Challenger Expedition (1872-1876)
teaser: The HMS Challenger spent four years sailing 68,000 nautical miles, dredging the deep sea for the first time and discovering life where science said none could exist. Its crew sounded the deepest points of the oceans and collected thousands of new species. The expedition founded the science of oceanography.
byline: The crew of the HMS Challenger

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the expedition mapped the ocean floor, then trace how its findings overturned the belief that the deep sea was lifeless.

name: The Mariana Trench Descent (1960)
teaser: Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh took the bathyscaphe Trieste 35,797 feet down to the bottom of the Mariana Trench — deeper than any humans before or since. They spent twenty minutes on the ocean floor, spotting a fish and a shrimp in the eternal dark. The descent proved life could survive the greatest pressure on Earth.

exploreAction.targetName: the Trieste descent to the Mariana Trench
exploreAction.instruction: Read how the bathyscaphe was built to survive unimaginable pressure, then consider what the dive revealed about the deep sea.

name: The D-Day Landings (1944)
teaser: On June 6, 1944, 156,000 Allied troops crossed the English Channel in the largest amphibious invasion in history. Omaha Beach came closest to disaster; by nightfall the Allies held the beaches and the liberation of Western Europe had begun. Within a year, Germany surrendered.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the invasion was planned in secret and executed under fire, then trace the breakout from Normandy to the fall of Berlin.

name: Operation Barbarossa (1941)
teaser: On June 22, 1941, Hitler launched the largest military invasion in history — three million men, 3,000 tanks, and 4,000 aircraft against the Soviet Union. The Wehrmacht advanced to Moscow's outskirts before winter and Soviet counterattacks stopped it. The campaign became the war's decisive front, where Germany lost a million men in the first year alone.
byline: Nazi Germany vs. the Soviet Union

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the invasion was planned as a quick war and became a grinding one, then trace the battles that turned the tide — Moscow, Stalingrad, Kursk.

name: The Suez Crisis (1956)
teaser: Egypt's Nasser nationalized the Suez Canal, and Britain, France, and Israel invaded to take it back — only to be forced into a humiliating retreat by American and Soviet pressure. The crisis marked the end of Britain and France as imperial powers in the Middle East. It confirmed the United States and the Soviet Union as the region's new arbiters.
byline: Britain, France, and Israel vs. Egypt

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the secret collusion was exposed, then trace how the crisis redrew Middle Eastern power and ended old European empires.

name: Operation Overlord's Planning (1943-1944)
teaser: The invasion of Normandy took a year of planning: artificial harbors, a secret army of decoys, and the largest deception campaign in history — Operation Fortitude — that convinced Hitler the landing would come at Calais. Double agents fed the Germans fake intelligence until D-Day itself. The plan's success sealed the invasion.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the deception campaign fooled German intelligence, then trace how logistics — from Mulberry harbors to PLUTO pipelines — made the invasion work.

name: The Civil Rights Movement (1954-1968)
teaser: From Brown v. Board of Education to the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr., the Civil Rights Movement dismantled legal segregation in America. Montgomery bus boycotts, sit-ins, Freedom Rides, and the Selma marches forced federal action — the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965. The movement's methods of nonviolent protest became a global template.
byline: Martin Luther King Jr., Rosa Parks, and millions of Americans

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the movement's campaigns escalated from courts to streets, then examine the backlash and the unfinished agenda it left.

name: The Anti-Apartheid Movement (1948-1994)
teaser: South Africa's white minority government institutionalized racial segregation as apartheid, and a global movement rose to oppose it — boycotts, sanctions, and the ANC's armed and peaceful resistance. Nelson Mandela's imprisonment made him the movement's symbol; his release in 1990 led to negotiations. Apartheid ended with the 1994 election that made Mandela president.
byline: The ANC and the international movement

exploreAction.instruction: Read how apartheid was built and how resistance grew, then trace the negotiated transition that brought majority rule.

name: The Women's Liberation Movement (1960s-1980s)
teaser: Second-wave feminism fought for equality in work, law, and the bedroom — equal pay, abortion rights, childcare, and an end to workplace discrimination. Betty Friedan's Feminine Mystique, the pill, and the ERA campaign animated a generation. The movement won legal changes across the West, even where it lost its headline battles.
byline: The feminist organizers of the 1960s and 70s

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the movement turned personal grievances into political demands, then trace its victories and the backlash it provoked.

name: The Green Revolution (1940s-1960s)
teaser: New high-yield wheat and rice varieties, developed by Norman Borlaug and others, roughly doubled global grain production and helped feed a billion more people. The revolution's fertilizer and irrigation came with environmental costs, and its benefits bypassed the poorest. Borlaug's work earned the Nobel Peace Prize — and a legacy of debate.
byline: Norman Borlaug and the agricultural scientists

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the new varieties and inputs raised yields, then weigh the revolution's trade-offs between production and environment.

name: The Open-Source Movement (1980s-present)
teaser: What began as Richard Stallman's fight for free software grew into the open-source movement: Linux, the Apache web server, and the software that runs much of the internet. Developers share code openly, and thousands contribute to projects like Python and Kubernetes. The movement challenged how software — and knowledge itself — is owned.
byline: Richard Stallman, Linus Torvalds, and the developer community

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the free software philosophy became open-source practice, then trace how open collaboration built the modern internet.

name: The 2008 Financial Crisis
teaser: When American subprime mortgages collapsed, the global financial system nearly froze — Lehman Brothers failed, and governments spent trillions bailing out banks 'too big to fail.' Millions lost homes and jobs, and the crisis birthed Occupy Wall Street and a wave of populism. Its regulatory aftermath, Dodd-Frank, sought to prevent a repeat.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how mortgage-backed securities spread risk through the system, then trace the panic, the bailouts, and the political aftershocks.

name: The Eurozone Debt Crisis (2009-2015)
teaser: Greece's hidden debts detonated a crisis that threatened the euro itself, as Ireland, Portugal, Spain, and Italy came under market pressure. The EU and the IMF mounted bailouts that came with austerity — cuts that triggered protests and political earthquakes. The crisis exposed the euro's design flaw: a shared currency without a shared fiscal policy.
byline: The EU, the IMF, and the debtor states

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Greece's deficits and the markets' panic escalated, then trace the austerity, bailouts, and reforms that stabilized the euro.

name: The Cuban Revolution's Aftermath: The Bay of Pigs (1961)
teaser: A CIA-trained invasion force of Cuban exiles landed at the Bay of Pigs expecting a popular uprising — and was crushed by Castro's army in three days. The disaster embarrassed Kennedy, hardened Castro's alliance with Moscow, and emboldened the Soviets to place missiles in Cuba. The failure was the prelude to the missile crisis of 1962.
byline: The CIA and the Cuban exiles

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the invasion plan unraveled when the promised air support and uprising failed, then trace its consequences for the Cold War.

name: The Falklands War (1982)
teaser: Argentina's military junta invaded the Falkland Islands, believing Britain would not fight for a distant colony. Britain's task force sailed 8,000 miles, retook the islands in ten weeks, and sank the Argentine cruiser Belgrano. The victory saved Thatcher's government and toppled the Argentine junta.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the task force was assembled and fought, then trace the war's political consequences in both countries.

name: The Romantic Movement (late 18th-19th century)
teaser: In reaction to Enlightenment rationalism, Romanticism exalted emotion, nature, and the individual genius. Wordsworth and Goethe in literature, Turner and Delacroix in painting, and Chopin and Beethoven in music all rejected cold rules for passionate feeling. The movement reshaped how the West thought about art, love, and the self.
byline: The poets, painters, and composers of Europe

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the movement reacted against the Enlightenment and industrialization, then trace its influence from poetry to nationalism and beyond.

name: The Labor Movement (19th-20th century)
teaser: As industrialization concentrated wealth, workers organized unions and parties to demand the eight-hour day, safety laws, and the vote. From the Luddites to the Haymarket strike to the founding of labor parties, the movement fought for the rights now taken for granted. Its victories — weekends, minimum wages, workplace safety — remade industrial society.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the movement grew from machine-breaking to mass politics, then trace its peak and decline in the late 20th century.

name: The Temperance Movement (19th-early 20th century)
teaser: A moral crusade against alcohol, driven by women's groups and churches, grew from personal pledge to national law — Prohibition in the United States from 1920 to 1933. The movement's supporters saw drink as the cause of poverty, violence, and family ruin. Prohibition proved unenforceable and was repealed, but the movement shaped drinking culture for generations.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the movement won the Eighteenth Amendment, then examine why enforcement failed and how the experiment ended.

name: The Pan-African Movement (1900-present)
teaser: From W.E.B. Du Bois's first Pan-African Congress to the independence of dozens of African states, the movement united people of African descent against colonialism and racism. It gave intellectual force to decolonization and inspired leaders from Kwame Nkrumah to Nelson Mandela. Its dream of African unity remains a work in progress.
byline: Du Bois, Nkrumah, and the movement's leaders

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the congresses moved from London to the African continent, then trace the movement's role in decolonization and the African Union.

name: The Conservation Movement (19th-20th century)
teaser: John Muir's fight to save Yosemite and Theodore Roosevelt's national parks made preservation a national project, while Gifford Pinchot's 'wise use' philosophy framed conservation as management. The movement saved the Grand Canyon, the sequoias, and the bison. Its heirs — the EPA, Earth Day, and modern environmentalism — grew from these roots.
byline: John Muir, Theodore Roosevelt, and the conservationists

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the movement split between preservation and management, then trace its evolution from parks to environmental law.

name: The American Indian Movement (1968-present)
teaser: Founded in 1968 to fight police brutality and treaty violations, AIM grew into the voice of Native resistance — the occupation of Alcatraz, the Trail of Broken Treaties, and the siege at Wounded Knee in 1973. The movement forced the nation to confront the history of dispossession. Its legacy lives in the fight for tribal sovereignty.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the movement's occupations brought Native grievances to national attention, then trace its impact on tribal rights and identity.

name: The Rosetta Stone Discovery (1799)
teaser: A French soldier found a slab near Rosetta, Egypt, inscribed with the same decree in hieroglyphs, demotic, and Greek — the key that unlocked ancient Egyptian writing. Jean-François Champollion cracked the hieroglyphs in 1822 using the Ptolemy cartouche. The stone turned Egyptology from guesswork into a science.
byline: Champollion and the scholars of the decipherment

exploreAction.targetName: the Rosetta Stone and the decipherment of hieroglyphs
exploreAction.instruction: Read how the three scripts provided the key, then follow Champollion's breakthrough that opened three thousand years of Egyptian history.

name: The Discovery of Penicillin (1928)
teaser: Alexander Fleming returned from holiday to find mold had killed the bacteria in a forgotten petri dish. It took a decade and the work of Florey and Chain to turn his 'mold juice' into a drug. Penicillin saved millions of lives in World War II and launched the antibiotic era — and the antibiotic-resistance crisis that followed.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the accidental mold became a medicine, then trace the mass production that made penicillin the first miracle drug.

name: The Discovery of DNA's Structure (1953)
teaser: James Watson and Francis Crick, using Rosalind Franklin's X-ray photographs without her consent, built the double-helix model of DNA in 1953. The structure explained how life copies itself — and opened genetics, forensics, and biotechnology. Franklin's excluded role became one of science's most examined injustices.

exploreAction.targetName: the discovery of the structure of DNA
exploreAction.instruction: Read how the race to the double helix was run, then consider the controversial question of who deserves the credit.

name: The Discovery of the Dead Sea Scrolls Cave 4 (1949)
teaser: The richest cache of Dead Sea Scrolls, thousands of fragments from over 500 manuscripts, was found in a cave near Qumran in 1949. The fragments include every book of the Hebrew Bible except Esther, some a thousand years older than previous copies. Their study revolutionized the history of the biblical text.
byline: The archaeologists of the Qumran caves

exploreAction.targetName: the Dead Sea Scrolls of Cave 4
exploreAction.instruction: Read what the cave's manuscripts revealed about the Bible's transmission, then consider the decades-long scholarly fight over their publication.

name: The Discovery of Fire's Mastery (c. 400,000-1,000,000 years ago)
teaser: The controlled use of fire was humanity's first great energy technology — warmth, light, cooked food, and defense against predators. Cooking expanded the calories our ancestors could digest, feeding bigger brains. The mastery of fire, wherever and whenever it happened, set the human story apart from every other species.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the archaeological evidence for early hearths, then trace how fire transformed diet, social life, and survival.

name: The Fate of the Roanoke Colony (1587-1590)
teaser: The English colony on Roanoke Island vanished while its governor was away for three years — the only clue the word 'Croatoan' carved on a post. Hardship, dispersal among native peoples, or disaster: no one knows. The Lost Colony remains America's oldest unsolved mystery, and every generation finds new evidence and new theories.

exploreAction.targetName: the mystery of the Roanoke Colony
exploreAction.instruction: Read the evidence — the carved word, the reports, the archaeology — then weigh the theories about where the colonists went.

name: The Fate of the Amber Room (1941-1945)
teaser: The Amber Room, a chamber paneled in six tons of amber given to Peter the Great, was looted by Nazi troops from Catherine Palace and shipped to Königsberg. It vanished during the war's final chaos and has never been found. Hunters have chased rumors of it in bunkers, mines, and the Baltic Sea for eighty years.
byline: The Nazis and the treasure hunters

exploreAction.targetName: the mystery of the Amber Room
exploreAction.instruction: Read how the room was dismantled and what happened to it last, then follow the searches and the leading theories about its fate.

name: The Voynich Manuscript (c. 1404-1438)
teaser: A hand-written book of unknown script, strange plants, and astronomical charts has defied every codebreaker for a century. Carbon dating places its vellum in the 1400s; no one knows who wrote it, what language it encodes, or whether it is a real cipher or an elaborate hoax. It lives at Yale, and its mystery remains intact.

exploreAction.instruction: Read what the manuscript contains and the attempts to decode it, then weigh the evidence for cipher versus hoax.

name: The Mary Celeste (1872)
teaser: The brig Mary Celeste was found adrift off the Azores, sails set, cargo intact, and lifeboat missing — but no sign of her captain, family, or crew of ten. The last log entry was ten days earlier. Theories range from mutiny to explosion to a waterspout. The ship's fate became the most famous maritime mystery of all time.
byline: The crew of the Mary Celeste

exploreAction.targetName: the mystery of the Mary Celeste
exploreAction.instruction: Read the known facts of the abandoned ship, then examine the theories — and why the simplest one may be the likeliest.

name: The Phaistos Disc (c. 1700 BCE)
teaser: A fired-clay disc stamped with a spiral of 241 symbols in a script found nowhere else was unearthed in Crete in 1908. Its language, meaning, and even authenticity are debated — no second example has ever been found. It remains one of archaeology's most tantalizing unsolved inscriptions.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the arguments over the disc's origin and meaning, then consider what the world's first 'printed' text might have said.

name: The Gallic Wars (58-50 BCE)
teaser: Julius Caesar spent eight years conquering Gaul — modern France and Belgium — in a campaign he narrated himself in Commentaries on the Gallic War. His conquest brought the region into the Roman world and gave Caesar the wealth and legions to cross the Rubicon. The final battle at Alesia, where he besieged and defeated Vercingetorix, sealed Gaul's fate.

exploreAction.instruction: Read Caesar's own account of the campaigns, then trace how the conquest of Gaul made his rise to power possible.

name: The Reconquista (718-1492)
teaser: For nearly eight centuries, Christian kingdoms in Iberia slowly pushed the Muslim states of al-Andalus southward in a war of religion, territory, and identity. The long campaign ended in 1492 when Granada fell and the Catholic Monarchs expelled the last Muslim rulers — and soon after, the Jews. The Reconquista shaped Spanish identity and empire.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the frontier moved back and forth for centuries, then trace the 1492 conquest of Granada and its aftermath.

name: Napoleon's Invasion of Russia (1812)
teaser: Napoleon marched 600,000 men into Russia; fewer than 100,000 came back. The Grande Armée reached Moscow only to find it burning, then retreated through the Russian winter, losing most of its men to cold, hunger, and Cossack attacks. The disaster destroyed Napoleon's invincibility and began his empire's unraveling.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the Russian scorched-earth strategy and winter destroyed the army, then trace how 1812 set up Napoleon's final fall.

name: The Winter Offensive: Sherman's March to the Sea (1864)
teaser: From Atlanta to Savannah, William Tecumseh Sherman's 60,000 men cut a 60-mile swath through Georgia, destroying railroads, mills, and plantations — 'making Georgia howl.' The march broke the Confederacy's will and economy and ended at Savannah in December 1864. Its 'total war' strategy remains controversial to this day.
byline: William Tecumseh Sherman and his army

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the march was planned as psychological warfare, then weigh its destruction against its role in ending the war.

name: The New Deal (1933-1939)
teaser: Franklin Roosevelt's alphabet of agencies — WPA, CCC, TVA, SEC, Social Security — answered the Great Depression by putting millions to work and regulating the economy. The New Deal built dams, bridges, parks, and post offices, and created the modern safety net. Its legacy — big government, union rights, social insurance — still shapes American politics.
byline: Franklin D. Roosevelt and the New Dealers

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the programs attacked unemployment and instability, then trace the New Deal's lasting institutions and its political legacy.

name: The Great Leap Forward (1958-1962)
teaser: Mao Zedong's crash industrialization drive ordered peasants into communes and backyard steel furnaces to outproduce Britain. The resulting chaos, mismanagement, and diversion of labor produced a famine that killed tens of millions. The catastrophe was hidden from the Chinese people for years — and remains a forbidden subject in China today.
byline: Mao Zedong and the Communist Party

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the campaign's targets caused the famine, then examine why its scale was hidden and how China has dealt with the memory.

name: The Apollo Program (1961-1972)
teaser: Kennedy's 1961 pledge to land a man on the Moon by the decade's end drove NASA's Apollo program — at its peak consuming four percent of the federal budget. Six missions landed twelve astronauts on the Moon between 1969 and 1972. The program's technology, from integrated circuits to freeze-dried food, reshaped the modern world.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the program went from disaster — the Apollo 1 fire — to the Moon in eight years, then trace its technological fallout.

name: The Axial Age (c. 800-200 BCE)
teaser: In a few centuries, independent thinkers across Eurasia — Confucius and Laozi in China, the Buddha in India, the Hebrew prophets, and the Greek philosophers — asked the same question: how should humans live? Their answers became the world's great traditions. Historian Karl Jaspers called the period the Axial Age.
byline: The sages of Greece, India, China, and Israel

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the age's thinkers arose separately yet asked similar questions, then trace how their ideas still frame human ethics.

name: The Northern Song Renaissance (960-1127)
teaser: The Northern Song dynasty presided over the most advanced economy on Earth — paper money, movable type, gunpowder, and a navy that ruled the seas. Its scholars created the imperial examination culture and its artists painted landscapes of astonishing subtlety. The dynasty fell to the Jurchen, but its technological lead shaped the world.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Song China led the world in technology and commerce, then trace the inventions — printing, paper money, gunpowder — that transformed Eurasia.

name: The Age of Sail (1571-1862)
teaser: For three centuries, wind drove the world: the galleons of the Spanish treasure fleets, the East Indiamen of the trading companies, and the ships of the line that decided imperial wars. Sail moved the spices, silver, and slaves that built the modern world. The era ended when steam made wind obsolete.
byline: The sailors and shipbuilders of the maritime powers

exploreAction.instruction: Read how sailing ships and navigation made global trade possible, then trace the transition from canvas to steam power.

name: The Belle Époque (1871-1914)
teaser: Between the Franco-Prussian War and World War I, Paris — and Europe — enjoyed a golden age of peace, art, and invention. The Eiffel Tower rose, Impressionism and Art Nouveau flourished, and the cinema, the automobile, and the airplane were born. The glitter concealed the tensions that would erupt in 1914.
byline: The artists, inventors, and city-dwellers of Europe

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the era's peace and prosperity produced its culture, then notice the nationalist and imperial rivalries beneath the surface.

name: The Weimar Republic (1918-1933)
teaser: Germany's first democracy was born of defeat and died of depression. The republic survived coups, hyperinflation — a loaf of bread costing billions of marks — and produced the culture of Expressionism, Bauhaus, and cabaret. The Depression's misery let the Nazis exploit the system from within and destroy it.
byline: The politicians and citizens of Weimar Germany

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the republic's constitution and culture thrived amid crisis, then trace the spiral from inflation to the Nazi seizure of power.

name: The Swinging Sixties (1960s)
teaser: A decade of protest and liberation: civil rights, the counterculture, the pill, and the Beatles. Youth culture went global for the first time, and authority — governments, parents, conventions — was questioned everywhere. The decade's hopes crashed at Altamont and in the Vietnam quagmire, but its cultural changes were permanent.
byline: The young people of the West

exploreAction.instruction: Read how music, protest, and affluence interacted, then weigh the decade's achievements against its disappointments.

name: The Thirty Years' War's Peace: The Peace of Prague? (1635)
teaser: A decade and a half into the Thirty Years' War, the Peace of Prague briefly reunited the German princes with the emperor against foreign invaders. It failed to end the war — France and Sweden kept fighting — but it showed how religion had given way to power politics. The war would run another thirteen years.
byline: The emperor and the German princes

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the peace realigned the war's coalitions, then trace why it failed to end the catastrophe.

name: The War of 1812 (1812-1815)
teaser: Fought between the young United States and Britain over trade restrictions, impressment, and expansion — and declared by Congress after Britain's blockade of Europe reached American ships. The war ended in a draw, but Andrew Jackson's New Orleans victory came after peace was signed. The burning of Washington and the Star-Spangled Banner both belong to the war.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the war was fought on land, sea, and the Great Lakes, then consider why Americans remember it as a second independence.

name: The Spanish Civil War (1936-1939)
teaser: A military coup against the Spanish Republic exploded into a three-year civil war that became a rehearsal for World War II. Fascist Italy and Nazi Germany backed Franco; the Soviet Union backed the Republic, which also drew volunteer International Brigades. Picasso's Guernica memorialized the bombing of a Basque town. Franco ruled Spain until 1975.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how foreign powers intervened in the war, then examine Guernica and the war's place as a prelude to the world conflict.

name: The Six-Day War (1967)
teaser: In six days, Israel destroyed the air forces of Egypt, Syria, and Jordan and seized the Sinai, the Golan Heights, the West Bank, and East Jerusalem. The preemptive strike followed years of rising tensions and the closure of the Straits of Tiran. The war redrew the Middle East's map — and its occupation of the territories shapes the region to this day.
byline: Israel vs. Egypt, Syria, and Jordan

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the preemptive strike decided the war in its first hours, then trace the war's territorial and political consequences.

name: The Iran-Iraq War (1980-1988)
teaser: Saddam Hussein invaded Iran, expecting a quick victory over the revolution's chaos; instead the war ground on for eight years with trench warfare, chemical weapons, and half a million to a million dead. Neither side won; the war bankrupted both. Its legacy — including Iraq's weapons programs and Iran's militarization — echoed for decades.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the war degenerated into attrition and chemical attacks, then trace its consequences for both countries and the region.

name: The Discovery of Troy (1871)
teaser: Heinrich Schliemann, an amateur archaeologist armed with Homer, dug into a mound at Hisarlik in Turkey and claimed to have found the city of Troy — and 'Priam's Treasure.' His methods destroyed much of what he found, but he proved the city was real. Later excavations revealed a site occupied for thousands of years.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Schliemann's obsession led him to Hisarlik, then weigh what his excavations found, destroyed, and left for later archaeologists.

name: The Discovery of the Titanic Wreck (1985)
teaser: Seventy-three years after the ship sank, Robert Ballard's expedition found the Titanic's remains two and a half miles down in the North Atlantic. The discovery transformed deep-sea archaeology and turned the wreck into a pilgrimage site — and a salvage battlefield. The ship's condition is deteriorating faster than anyone predicted.
byline: Robert Ballard and the Woods Hole team

exploreAction.targetName: the discovery of the Titanic wreck
exploreAction.instruction: Read how sonar and the search for a submarine pair found the wreck, then consider the debates over salvage versus preservation.

name: The Discovery of the First Exoplanets (1990s)
teaser: In 1995, astronomers announced a planet orbiting a sunlike star — 51 Pegasi b, a 'hot Jupiter' where a year lasts four days. Since then, thousands of exoplanets have been found, including Earth-sized worlds in habitable zones. The discovery that planets are everywhere changed our place in the cosmos.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the radial-velocity method caught the first exoplanet, then trace the explosion of discovery from Kepler to today.

name: The League of Nations (1920-1946)
teaser: Woodrow Wilson's dream of a world body to prevent war became the League of Nations — crippled from the start by the U.S. Senate's refusal to join. The League failed to stop Japan in Manchuria, Italy in Ethiopia, or Hitler's remilitarization. It dissolved during World War II, but its agencies and ideals seeded the United Nations.
byline: The member states of the League

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the League's structure and missing members limited it, then trace its failures and its institutional legacy.

name: Ramesses II (c. 1303-1213 BCE)
teaser: The pharaoh most associated with 'Moses and the exodus' ruled Egypt for 66 years, building Abu Simbel and siring over a hundred children. His treaty with the Hittites — the first recorded peace treaty — and his monuments made him Egypt's greatest self-publicist. His mummy still wears his red hair in the Cairo Museum.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Ramesses built and boasted on an unmatched scale, then trace the battle of Kadesh and the peace treaty that followed.

name: Cyrus the Great (c. 600-530 BCE)
teaser: The founder of the Persian Empire conquered the Medes, Babylon, and much of the ancient Near East — and ruled with a tolerance almost unknown in his time. Cyrus freed the Jews of Babylon, as the Bible records, and let conquered peoples keep their gods. His empire's model of governance shaped every later empire, including Rome.

exploreAction.targetName: the reign of Cyrus the Great
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Cyrus built the largest empire of his time, then examine his cylinder — often called the first charter of human rights.

name: Augustus (63 BCE - 14 CE)
teaser: The first Roman emperor inherited a republic torn by civil war and gave it peace — the Pax Romana. He called himself 'first citizen' rather than king, rebuilt Rome in marble, and created the institutions that ran the empire for two centuries. His reign, from Actium in 31 BCE to his death, set the mold for every later emperor.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Augustus disguised autocracy as restoration, then trace the reforms that made the empire work.

name: Saladin (1137-1193)
teaser: The Kurdish sultan who united the Muslim Near East and recaptured Jerusalem from the Crusaders in 1187 was renowned on both sides for his chivalry. He spared the city's Christians when the Crusaders had massacred its Muslims. His wars with Richard the Lionheart became legend — and his example still shapes how both faiths remember the Crusades.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Saladin united Egypt and Syria, then follow the siege of Jerusalem and the truce with Richard that ended the Third Crusade.

name: Queen Elizabeth I (1533-1603)
teaser: The last Tudor monarch survived plots, invasions, and a court of suitors to rule England for 45 years. Her defeat of the Armada, her religious settlement, and her patronage of Shakespeare made her reign England's golden age. She never married — the 'Virgin Queen' — and turned her singleness into a political weapon.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Elizabeth managed Parliament, religion, and the marriage market, then trace the crises — Mary Queen of Scots, the Armada — she survived.

name: The Georgian Era (1714-1837)
teaser: Four kings named George ruled Britain through the age of empire, industrialization, and revolution. The era saw the loss of the American colonies, the victory over Napoleon, and the transformation of Britain into the workshop of the world. Georgian London grew from a city of 600,000 to a metropolis of two million.
byline: The Hanoverian kings and Georgian Britain

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the era's wars and trade built the British Empire, then trace the social changes from the enclosure of fields to the factory towns.

name: The Edo Period of Japan (1603-1868)
teaser: For 265 years, the Tokugawa shoguns sealed Japan from the outside world, and peace allowed culture to flower — kabuki, ukiyo-e, haiku, and the merchant culture of Edo. Society was rigidly ordered by class, yet the economy grew and literacy spread. The arrival of Perry's ships in 1853 shattered the seclusion and ended the era.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the peace of the era produced its culture, then trace the pressures — famine, samurai poverty, foreign ships — that ended it.

name: The Antebellum South (1815-1861)
teaser: The American South before the Civil War built a cotton empire on enslaved labor that made it the world's dominant cotton supplier. Its planter elite controlled politics, its economy remained agrarian, and its 'peculiar institution' deepened as the cotton gin spread. The era's contradictions — wealth, honor, and human bondage — exploded in 1861.
byline: The planters and enslaved people of the South

exploreAction.instruction: Read how cotton and slavery shaped the region's economy and politics, then trace the growing divide with the industrial North.

name: The Reconstruction Era (1865-1877)
teaser: After the Civil War, the federal government tried to rebuild the South and guarantee rights for the freed people — with the 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments. Black men voted, served in office, and built schools, until a backlash of terror and the Compromise of 1877 ended federal protection. The era's failure shaped a century of segregation.
byline: Congress, the presidents, and the freed people

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Reconstruction's promise was made and broken, then trace how its collapse produced Jim Crow.

name: The Interwar Years (1918-1939)
teaser: The twenty-one years between the world wars saw fragile peace, runaway inflation, the Jazz Age, and the Great Depression — and the rise of fascism across Europe. Democracies struggled, empires crumbled, and the League of Nations failed its first tests. The era's failure to manage its crises led straight to 1939.
byline: The democracies and dictatorships of Europe

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the peace settlements and the Depression destabilized Europe, then trace the path from the Rhineland to the Sudetenland to war.

name: The Enlightenment's Child: The Scottish Enlightenment (c. 1730-1800)
teaser: In a small, poor country, Edinburgh and Glasgow produced David Hume, Adam Smith, and James Watt — the philosopher, economist, and engineer who defined the modern world. The Scottish Enlightenment pioneered the social sciences, the free market, and modern technology. Its ideas crossed the Atlantic into the American founding.
byline: Hume, Smith, and the thinkers of Scotland

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Scotland's universities produced its thinkers, then trace how Smith's Wealth of Nations and Hume's empiricism shaped the West.

name: The Arts and Crafts Movement (1880-1910)
teaser: In reaction to ugly mass production, William Morris and his followers revived handcraft and honest materials — furniture, wallpaper, and buildings made by skilled hands. The movement's ideals of design quality and craft dignity influenced everything from architecture to the modern studio movement. Its founder declared: 'Have nothing in your houses that you do not know to be useful or believe to be beautiful.'

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the movement answered industrialization with craft, then trace its influence on Art Nouveau, the Bauhaus, and design ethics.

name: The Suffrage Movement in the United States (1848-1920)
teaser: From the Seneca Falls Convention of 1848 to the ratification of the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920, American women campaigned for the vote for 72 years. Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Susan B. Anthony, and a new generation including Alice Paul built the movement through petitions, parades, and prison. The final victory came only after the First World War.
byline: Stanton, Anthony, Paul, and the suffragists

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the movement's tactics evolved from the convention to the picket line, then trace the politics of the final ratification.

name: The Temperance Triumph: The Eighteenth Amendment (1919)
teaser: The culmination of a century of temperance campaigning, the Eighteenth Amendment banned the manufacture and sale of alcohol across the United States. Its supporters promised a more moral, productive nation. Within a decade, enforcement collapsed, crime boomed, and public opinion turned — leading to repeal in 1933, the only constitutional amendment ever revoked.
byline: The Anti-Saloon League and its allies

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the amendment passed and how it failed, then consider what the experiment says about legislating morality.

name: The Discovery of the Burgess Shale (1909)
teaser: Charles Walcott's discovery of a fossil bed in the Canadian Rockies revealed the bizarre fauna of the Cambrian explosion — animals like Opabinia with five eyes and Anomalocaris with claws for a mouth — perfectly preserved in soft-bodied detail. The shale changed our understanding of early life and evolution. It remains one of the world's most important fossil sites.

exploreAction.instruction: Read what the shale's soft-bodied fossils revealed, then consider how the 'weird wonders' challenged evolutionary thinking.

name: The Discovery of the Lascaux Caves (1940)
teaser: Four teenagers chasing a dog found a cave in southwestern France whose walls were painted with hundreds of animals — horses, deer, and bulls — some 17,000 years ago. The paintings are among the finest prehistoric art ever found. The cave was closed to the public in 1963 to preserve it; a perfect replica now receives visitors.

exploreAction.targetName: the discovery of the Lascaux Caves
exploreAction.instruction: Read what the paintings depict and how they were made, then consider what they suggest about the minds of early humans.

name: The Discovery of Lucy (1974)
teaser: In Ethiopia's Afar region, Donald Johanson's team found the skeleton of a 3.2-million-year-old hominid, 40 percent complete — named Lucy after the Beatles song playing that night. She walked upright, which changed the story of human evolution. Her species, Australopithecus afarensis, is among our oldest known ancestors.

exploreAction.instruction: Read what Lucy's skeleton revealed about upright walking, then trace the debates her discovery provoked about the human family tree.

name: The Battle of Cannae (216 BCE)
teaser: Hannibal's double envelopment at Cannae destroyed a Roman army of up to 80,000 — the worst defeat in Roman history and a textbook of encirclement still studied in military academies. The Romans refused to negotiate, and Hannibal could not finish the war. The battle became a byword for perfect tactics without strategic result.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the cavalry turned the flanks to encircle the Romans, then consider why even Cannae could not win the war.

name: The Battle of Adrianople (378 CE)
teaser: The Visigoths, fleeing the Huns, annihilated a Roman army at Adrianople and killed Emperor Valens — the first time a Gothic army destroyed a full Roman field army. The defeat exposed the empire's fragility and forced the Romans to settle the Goths inside imperial borders. It is often called the beginning of the end for the Western Empire.
byline: The Visigoths vs. the Roman Empire

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the Roman cavalry's absence and poor tactics doomed the army, then trace the battle's consequences for the empire's frontier.

name: The Battle of Zama (202 BCE)
teaser: Scipio Africanus finally met Hannibal in the field — and beat him, using the elephants that Hannibal had once used against Rome, funneled into gaps so they turned on their own lines. The defeat ended the Second Punic War and made Rome the master of the western Mediterranean. It was Hannibal's first and only defeat in Italy and Africa.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Scipio's adaptation of Carthaginian tactics won the day, then trace the peace that made Rome the Mediterranean's dominant power.

name: The Battle of Blenheim (1704)
teaser: The Duke of Marlborough and Prince Eugene smashed the Franco-Bavarian army at Blenheim, saving Vienna and shattering the myth of French invincibility. The victory ended the War of Spanish Succession's worst threat and made Marlborough the greatest general of his age. Britain's queen granted him Blenheim Palace — the birthplace of Winston Churchill.
byline: Marlborough and Eugene vs. the Franco-Bavarian army

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Marlborough's forced march surprised the enemy, then trace how the victory changed the balance of European power.

name: The Battle of Jutland (1916)
teaser: The only full-scale clash of dreadnought fleets in history ended inconclusively: Britain lost more ships, Germany more men, and neither side won the sea. The German fleet never risked a full engagement again, leaving Britain's blockade intact. Jutland secured the naval dominance that slowly starved Germany into defeat.
byline: The British Grand Fleet vs. the German High Seas Fleet

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the fleets groped for each other in the mist, then weigh which side actually achieved its strategic aim.

name: Caesar's Crossing of the Rubicon (49 BCE)
teaser: By leading his legions across the Rubicon — the boundary of his province — Caesar committed treason and started a civil war. 'The die is cast,' he reportedly said. The crossing pitted Caesar against Pompey and the Senate, and his victory made him dictator for life. The phrase 'crossing the Rubicon' still means an irreversible decision.

exploreAction.instruction: Read why the crossing was an act of war, then trace the civil war from the Rubicon to Pharsalus and Caesar's dictatorship.

name: The Bataan Death March (1942)
teaser: After surrendering on Bataan, some 76,000 American and Filipino prisoners were forced to march 65 miles in tropical heat with no food or water. Thousands died of exhaustion, starvation, or execution by their Japanese captors. The march became a symbol of Japanese brutality and fueled Allied fury in the Pacific War.
byline: The Imperial Japanese Army and the prisoners of Bataan

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the march unfolded and its toll, then consider its place in the memory of the Pacific War and the trials that followed.

name: The Trail of Tears (1830-1850)
teaser: Under the Indian Removal Act, the U.S. government forced the Cherokee and other southeastern nations from their homelands to territory west of the Mississippi. The marches of the 1830s, especially the Cherokee removal of 1838-39, killed thousands through cold, hunger, and disease. The Trail of Tears remains the defining injustice of American expansion.
byline: The United States government and the Cherokee Nation

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the removal was justified and resisted, then trace the route and the toll of the forced marches.

name: The Republic of Venice's Arsenal (1104-1797)
teaser: The Arsenal of Venice was the greatest industrial complex of the medieval world, mass-producing ships with assembly-line efficiency — a galley could be built in a day. Its cannons, rope works, and foundries made Venice's navy the terror of the Mediterranean. Dante visited it; the word 'arsenal' comes from its Arabic-rooted name.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the Arsenal pioneered mass production centuries before the factory, then trace its role in Venice's naval power.

name: The Kingdom of Aksum (c. 100-940 CE)
teaser: One of the great powers of the ancient world, Aksum controlled the Red Sea trade between the Roman Empire and India, minted its own gold coins, and converted to Christianity in the 4th century. Its obelisks, its church at Axum, and its claim to hold the Ark of the Covenant still define Ethiopian identity. The kingdom's decline followed the rise of Islam's trade routes.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Aksum's trade and Christianity made it a power, then trace its legacy in Ethiopian civilization and the legend of the Ark.

name: The Khazar Khaganate (c. 650-969)
teaser: The Khazars, a Turkic people of the steppe, built a powerful state between the Caspian and Black Seas and, uniquely in medieval history, adopted Judaism as their elite religion. They held the line between Christendom and the caliphate, taxing the trade routes. Their fate — absorbed by Rus and Byzantine pressure — is debated, and their conversion still fascinates historians.
byline: The Khagan and the Khazar elite

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the Khazars balanced empires and converted to Judaism, then examine the theories about their disappearance.

name: The Ottoman Millet System (1453-1920s)
teaser: The Ottoman Empire governed its diverse subjects through millets — religious communities that ran their own courts, schools, and charities under their own laws. Christians, Jews, and Muslims coexisted for centuries under this arrangement, paying taxes in return for autonomy. The millet system's communal logic would both protect and divide the empire's peoples.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the millets balanced tolerance and hierarchy, then trace how the system's divisions were exploited as the empire declined.

name: The Indian Caste System (c. 1500 BCE-present)
teaser: Born from ancient Vedic texts, the caste system divided Indian society into hereditary groups — priests, warriors, merchants, laborers, and the 'untouchables' outside the system entirely. It shaped marriage, work, and worship for three millennia. Constitutional abolition and social movements have weakened it, but caste remains a living force in India's politics and society.
byline: The priestly and political authorities of India

exploreAction.instruction: Read how caste was codified and enforced, then examine the reform movements and laws that have challenged it.

name: The 2011 Tōhoku Earthquake and Tsunami
teaser: A magnitude 9.0 earthquake off Japan's northeast coast triggered a tsunami that killed nearly 20,000 people and overwhelmed the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant, causing meltdowns. The disaster was the most expensive in history, costing over $200 billion. It forced Japan to reexamine its nuclear program and its disaster preparedness.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the earthquake, tsunami, and nuclear failure compounded, then examine Japan's response and the global debate over nuclear power.

name: The Hurricane Katrina Disaster (2005)
teaser: When Hurricane Katrina struck New Orleans, the city's levees failed and 80 percent of the city flooded, killing 1,800 people — most of them poor and Black. The slow federal response and the images of stranded residents exposed systemic failure. The disaster sparked a decade of debate about race, poverty, and infrastructure.
byline: The federal government and the city of New Orleans

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the levee system failed and the evacuation fell short, then trace the storm's political and social aftermath.

name: The Discovery of the Double Helix of RNA (1950s)
teaser: The discovery that RNA — not just DNA — carries genetic information transformed biology, leading to the genetic code and biotechnology. RNA's roles — messenger, transfer, and the catalytic core of ribosomes — make it biology's most versatile molecule. The 'RNA world' hypothesis even proposes RNA came before DNA and life itself.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how RNA's functions were mapped, then consider the RNA world hypothesis about the origins of life.

name: The Discovery of the Antarctic Ozone Hole (1985)
teaser: British scientists at Halley Station found that the ozone layer over Antarctica had thinned by forty percent each spring — the result of CFCs in spray cans and refrigerators. The 1987 Montreal Protocol banned the chemicals, the first truly global environmental treaty. The ozone layer is now healing, proving collective action can fix a planetary problem.

exploreAction.targetName: the discovery of the ozone hole
exploreAction.instruction: Read how the measurements revealed the thinning and how CFCs were identified, then trace the Montreal Protocol's success.

name: The Discovery of the Higgs Boson (2012)
teaser: The Large Hadron Collider at CERN found the last missing piece of the Standard Model — the Higgs boson, the particle that gives other particles mass. The discovery confirmed a theory proposed in 1964 and earned Higgs and Englert the Nobel Prize. It was the largest, most expensive experiment in the history of science.

exploreAction.targetName: the discovery of the Higgs boson
exploreAction.instruction: Read how the collider was built and how the particle was detected, then consider what the Higgs means for physics — and what questions remain.

name: King Hammurabi (c. 1810-1750 BCE)
teaser: The sixth king of Babylon's First Dynasty created one of the earliest and best-preserved law codes in history — 282 laws carved on a seven-foot stele. 'An eye for an eye' is his best-known principle, though the code also set wages, prices, and liability for builders and surgeons. The stele, found in 1901, stands in the Louvre.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the code's laws and the logic behind them, then consider how the stele used law to project royal power.

name: Pericles (c. 495-429 BCE)
teaser: Athens's greatest statesman led the city through its golden age, building the Parthenon and delivering the Funeral Oration that defined democracy's ideals. Under his leadership, Athens ruled its empire, funded its arts, and prosecuted its war with Sparta. The plague killed him in 429 BCE — and took the golden age with him.

exploreAction.instruction: Read Pericles's Funeral Oration as Thucydides recorded it, then trace how his imperial ambition led Athens into the Peloponnesian War.

name: Cleopatra VII (69-30 BCE)
teaser: The last active pharaoh of Egypt was a brilliant politician who spoke a dozen languages and allied herself with Rome's two most powerful men — Julius Caesar and Mark Antony. Her defeat by Octavian at Actium ended both her reign and Ptolemaic Egypt. Her death by asp — or poison — became history's most famous suicide, and her legend outgrew her reality.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Cleopatra used her intellect and alliances to defend Egypt, then separate the historical queen from the Roman propaganda.

name: Alfred the Great (849-899)
teaser: The king of Wessex who saved England from Viking conquest, Alfred rebuilt his kingdom after near-total defeat and turned it into a military and cultural power. He translated Latin works into English, founded schools, and organized the defense that his successors used to unite England. He is the only English king called 'the Great.'

exploreAction.targetName: the reign of Alfred the Great
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Alfred's reforms rebuilt Wessex after the Viking wars, then trace how his dynasty united England.

name: Kublai Khan (1215-1294)
teaser: The grandson of Genghis Khan completed the Mongol conquest of China, founded the Yuan dynasty, and built the capital at Khanbaliq — modern Beijing. His court welcomed Marco Polo, and his empire stretched from the Pacific to the Danube. He failed twice to conquer Japan, saved by storms the Japanese called kamikaze — 'divine wind.'

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Kublai ruled the largest contiguous empire in history, then trace his failed invasions of Japan and Southeast Asia.

name: Mary Wollstonecraft (1759-1797)
teaser: The author of A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792) argued that women's apparent inferiority was the product of education, not nature — a radical claim in the revolutionary era. Her ideas shaped the suffrage movement a century later. She died days after giving birth to Mary Shelley, author of Frankenstein.

exploreAction.targetName: the life and ideas of Mary Wollstonecraft
exploreAction.instruction: Read the arguments of the Vindication, then trace her influence on the feminism that followed her.

name: Frederick Douglass (1818-1895)
teaser: Born into slavery, Douglass taught himself to read, escaped, and became the most famous Black American of the 19th century. His 1845 Narrative, his speeches against slavery, and his work for abolition, women's rights, and Reconstruction made him a moral authority. He never stopped arguing that the American promise belonged to everyone.

exploreAction.instruction: Read Douglass's narrative and his famous speeches, then trace his long career from abolitionist to statesman.

name: Marie Curie (1867-1934)
teaser: The only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences — physics in 1903 and chemistry in 1911 — Curie discovered radium and polonium and pioneered research into radioactivity. She coined the term 'radioactivity' and her work launched both nuclear physics and cancer radiotherapy. She died of aplastic anemia caused by her lifelong exposure to radiation.

exploreAction.targetName: the life and science of Marie Curie
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Curie's work on radiation opened a new field of physics and medicine, then trace the costs her discoveries demanded.

name: The Suffrage Milestone: Women Vote in New Zealand (1893)
teaser: New Zealand became the first self-governing country to grant women the vote in 1893, after a campaign led by Kate Sheppard and buoyed by the temperance movement. The victory inspired suffragists in Britain, America, and Australia. Sheppard's portrait appears on the New Zealand ten-dollar note.
byline: Kate Sheppard and the New Zealand suffragists

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the campaign won the world's first national women's vote, then trace its influence on the global movement.

name: The Labor Day Origins: The Haymarket Affair (1886)
teaser: A strike for the eight-hour day turned violent when a bomb was thrown at police in Chicago's Haymarket Square. The ensuing panic, trials, and executions of four anarchists — whose guilt was never proven — made May Day an international workers' holiday. The affair galvanized the American labor movement and its foes alike.
byline: The workers and the police of Chicago

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the bomb and the trials unfolded, then trace how the affair shaped May Day and the labor movement.

name: The Battle of the Sexes Moment: The Seneca Falls Convention (1848)
teaser: The first women's rights convention in the United States met at Seneca Falls, New York, and issued a Declaration of Sentiments modeled on the Declaration of Independence — 'all men and women are created equal.' The demand for suffrage passed narrowly. The convention is considered the formal start of the American women's rights movement.
byline: Stanton, Mott, and the convention organizers

exploreAction.instruction: Read the Declaration of Sentiments and its resolutions, then trace how the convention's demands were pursued over the next seven decades.

name: The Smithsonian Institution (1846)
teaser: Founded with the bequest of an English scientist who never visited America, the Smithsonian grew into the world's largest museum and research complex — nineteen museums, the National Zoo, and hundreds of research programs. Its collections hold the Star-Spangled Banner and the Wright Flyer. Its motto: 'the increase and diffusion of knowledge.'

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the bequest was accepted and built, then trace the institution's growth from a single castle to a national complex.

name: The Nobel Prize (1901)
teaser: Alfred Nobel, the inventor of dynamite, endowed prizes in physics, chemistry, medicine, literature, and peace — 'for the greatest benefit to humankind.' The first prizes were awarded in 1901, and the Nobel has become the world's most prestigious honor. The economics prize was added by the central bank in 1968.
byline: Alfred Nobel and the prize committees

exploreAction.targetName: the history of the Nobel Prize
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Nobel's will created the prizes and the controversies they still provoke, then trace the prize's evolution over a century.

name: The BBC (1922)
teaser: The British Broadcasting Corporation began as a radio monopoly and became the world's first and largest public broadcaster. Its charter obligations — to inform, educate, and entertain — and its independence from government set the model for public broadcasting. From wartime broadcasts to the World Service, the BBC shaped how Britain hears the world.
byline: John Reith and the founders of the BBC

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Reith's vision of public service broadcasting was built, then trace the BBC's evolution from radio to the internet age.

name: The Bronze Age (c. 3300-1200 BCE)
teaser: The discovery of bronze — an alloy of copper and tin — created the first metal age: swords, armor, and tools that let states rise and armies march. Trade networks reached across the Mediterranean and Near East to find tin. The Bronze Age's collapse around 1200 BCE ended the palaces, and the world fell back into centuries of iron and darkness.
byline: The metallurgists and states of the Bronze Age

exploreAction.instruction: Read how bronze technology reshaped warfare and society, then trace the trade networks and the age's mysterious collapse.

name: The Ice Age (c. 2.6 million - 10,000 years ago)
teaser: For most of human history, the planet was colder, with glaciers covering a third of the land and sea levels hundreds of feet lower. Early humans spread across the world during the Ice Age, crossing land bridges now under the ocean. The last ice age ended about 10,000 years ago — and the warming that followed made farming and civilization possible.
byline: The climate and the early humans

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the ice shaped migration and survival, then consider how the end of the ice age created the conditions for civilization.

name: The Great Depression's Decade: The 1930s
teaser: The 1930s were defined by economic collapse, dust, and the rise of fascism. America's New Deal built a safety net; Germany's crisis built a dictator. The decade's art — from Dorothea Lange's photographs to John Steinbeck's novels — recorded the human cost. By the decade's end, the world was arming for war.
byline: The people and governments of the 1930s

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the decade's crisis responses diverged — democracy, reform, and dictatorship — then trace the road to 1939.

name: The Republic of Texas (1836-1845)
teaser: Texas declared independence from Mexico in 1836 after the Alamo and San Jacinto, and existed as an independent republic for nine years — with its own president, currency, and star. Annexation by the United States in 1845 triggered the Mexican-American War. The republic's legend — the Alamo, Davy Crockett, 'Remember Goliad' — still defines Texas identity.
byline: Sam Houston and the Texian republicans

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the revolution was won at San Jacinto, then trace the republic's brief independence and annexation.

name: The Free City of Danzig (1920-1939)
teaser: Created by the Versailles Treaty as a semi-independent city-state under League of Nations protection, Danzig sat between Germany and the new Poland, with a Polish-controlled port and a German-majority population. Hitler's demand to annex it was the pretext for the invasion of Poland in 1939. The city's impossible position made it the fuse of the Second World War.
byline: The League of Nations and the peoples of Danzig

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the city's status was designed and why it failed, then trace its role in the outbreak of war.

name: The Edict of Milan (313 CE)
teaser: Constantine and his co-emperor Licinius proclaimed religious toleration for Christians across the Roman Empire, ending three centuries of persecution. The edict did not make Christianity the state religion — that came later — but it legalized the faith and returned confiscated property. Christianity's rise from a persecuted sect to the empire's dominant religion began here.

exploreAction.instruction: Read what the edict actually said and what it did not, then trace how the legalization transformed Christianity and the empire.

name: The Concordat of Worms (1122)
teaser: The Investiture Controversy — a half-century war between emperors and popes over who could appoint bishops — ended with a compromise: the emperor surrendered the ring and staff, but kept a role in secular investiture. The settlement weakened imperial authority and strengthened the papacy. It drew a line between church and state that Europe still argues over.
byline: Henry V and Pope Calixtus II

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the controversy began with Gregory VII and Henry IV at Canossa, then trace the compromise that ended it.

name: The Treaty of Ghent (1814)
teaser: The treaty that ended the War of 1812 restored the pre-war borders between the United States and British North America — a return to the status quo that resolved none of the war's stated causes. Neither side won, but the peace opened a century of mostly peaceful Anglo-American relations. News of the treaty traveled too slowly to stop the Battle of New Orleans.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the negotiations deadlocked and settled, then consider why a stalemate became the foundation of lasting peace.

name: The Convention of Kanagawa's Brother: The Treaty of Amity and Commerce (1858)
teaser: Commodore Perry's opening of Japan was completed by Townsend Harris, who negotiated the Harris Treaty of 1858 — opening four more ports, permitting trade, and granting extraterritoriality to foreigners. Japan's rejection of its terms fueled the anti-shogunate movement. The treaty ended Japan's isolation for good and set the country on its modern path.
byline: Townsend Harris and the Tokugawa shogunate

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the treaty's unequal terms outraged Japan, then trace how the humiliation produced the Meiji Restoration.

name: The Anglo-Japanese Alliance (1902)
teaser: Britain and Japan, both wary of Russia, signed the first alliance between a European and an Asian power. The alliance freed Japan to fight Russia in 1904 and let Britain concentrate its navy at home. It lasted twenty years, until the Washington Naval Treaty ended it. The alliance marked Japan's arrival as a great power.

exploreAction.instruction: Read why two island powers with no common border allied, then trace the alliance's role in the Russo-Japanese War.

name: The Treaty of San Francisco (1951)
teaser: The peace treaty ending the American occupation of Japan was signed by 48 nations in San Francisco, restoring Japanese sovereignty and renouncing its empire. The Soviet Union refused to sign, which is why Russia and Japan still lack a formal peace treaty. The settlement set Japan on its postwar path of pacifism and economic growth.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the treaty was shaped by the Cold War, then consider why the Soviet Union's refusal still blocks a Russian-Japanese peace.

name: The Battle of Gaugamela (331 BCE)
teaser: On an open plain, Alexander's cavalry wedge broke the Persian center and forced Darius III to flee, ending the Achaemenid Empire. Outnumbered perhaps three to one, Alexander won the battle that made him master of the ancient world. He then marched on Babylon, Susa, and Persepolis to claim the empire.
byline: Alexander the Great vs. Darius III

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Alexander's tactics exploited the gap in the Persian line, then trace the campaign that ended with Persepolis in flames.

name: The Battle of Pharsalus (48 BCE)
teaser: Caesar, outnumbered two to one, broke Pompey's superior army by holding back his reserve — a tactical surprise that decided the Roman civil war. Pompey fled to Egypt, where he was murdered on arrival. Caesar followed, met Cleopatra, and became master of Rome. The battle made Caesar's dictatorship inevitable.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Caesar's hidden reserve won the day, then trace the war's aftermath from Egypt to Caesar's assassination.

name: The Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa (1212)
teaser: A coalition of Christian kingdoms broke the Almohad army in the Sierra Morena mountains — the turning point of the Reconquista. The defeat destroyed Almohad power in Iberia and opened Andalusia to conquest. Within decades, the great cities of Cordoba and Seville fell to the Christians.
byline: The kings of Castile, Aragon, and Navarre

exploreAction.targetName: the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa
exploreAction.instruction: Read how the coalition stormed the mountain pass and broke the Almohads, then trace the conquest of Andalusia that followed.

name: The Battle of Vienna's Brother: The Battle of Lepanto (1571)
teaser: The last great naval battle fought with galleys saw the Christian Holy League destroy the Ottoman fleet off Greece. The victory broke the myth of Ottoman naval invincibility and saved the western Mediterranean from Ottoman dominance. Miguel de Cervantes, author of Don Quixote, lost the use of his left hand in the battle.
byline: The Holy League vs. the Ottoman fleet

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the fleets collided in the Gulf of Patras, then trace the battle's effect on Ottoman power and European confidence.

name: The Battle of Plassey (1757)
teaser: Robert Clive's 3,000 men defeated the Nawab of Bengal's 50,000 thanks to treachery in the nawab's own camp. The victory gave the East India Company control of Bengal — India's richest province — and the revenues to conquer the rest. Plassey is often called the founding battle of the British Empire in India.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the defection of Mir Jafar decided the battle, then trace how the victory turned a trading company into an empire.

name: The Battle of Plassey's Echo: The Siege of Delhi (1857)
teaser: During the Sepoy Rebellion, mutineers seized Delhi and proclaimed the Mughal emperor as their leader. British and loyalist forces besieged the city for months before storming it, executing the princes who had joined the revolt. The recapture of Delhi broke the rebellion's back and sealed the end of Mughal power and Company rule.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the mutiny's seizure of Delhi made it the war's symbolic center, then trace the brutal suppression that followed.

name: Alexander's Campaign in India (327-325 BCE)
teaser: Alexander pushed his army beyond the Indus and defeated King Porus at the Hydaspes, the only battle he ever came close to losing. His troops, exhausted after eight years, mutinied at the Beas and forced him to turn back. The retreat down the Indus and across the desert cost him most of the men he had left. His generals kept India; Alexander never saw Greece again.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the Hydaspes was won and why the army refused to go further, then trace the disastrous march home.

name: The Gothic War (535-554 CE)
teaser: Justinian's general Belisarius set out to recover Italy from the Ostrogoths and, after twenty years of war, famine, and plague, destroyed both the Gothic kingdom and Italy itself. Rome changed hands five times. The war's devastation helped end the classical world and opened Italy to the Lombard invasions that followed.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the reconquest was won and lost, then weigh the war's role in the ruin of late-antique Italy.

name: The Crusade of 1204: The Sack of Constantinople
teaser: The Fourth Crusade, diverted by Venetian money and Byzantine politics, ended not in Jerusalem but in the sack of Constantinople — a Christian city, by Christian crusaders. The empire's treasures were looted, its relics shipped west, and its people murdered. The sack of 1204 never healed; it sealed the schism between Orthodox and Catholic Christianity.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the crusade was hijacked by debts and intrigues, then trace the Byzantine recovery and the lasting schism.

name: The Late Middle Ages (c. 1300-1500)
teaser: The last two centuries of the medieval period were a time of crisis and transformation: the Black Death killed a third of Europe, the Hundred Years' War raged, and the papacy split. Yet the same era produced Chaucer, Giotto, and the first stirrings of the Renaissance. The old order was dying — and a new one was being born.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how plague, war, and schism shook the medieval order, then trace the recoveries that produced the Renaissance.

name: The Interregnum: Cromwell's Commonwealth (1649-1660)
teaser: After executing Charles I, Britain became a republic for eleven years, ruled by Parliament and then by Oliver Cromwell as Lord Protector. The Commonwealth conquered Ireland and Scotland but never won legitimacy at home. The experiment ended when Charles II was restored in 1660 — though the monarchy that returned was forever limited.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the republic governed and why it failed, then trace the restoration and its constitutional limits.

name: The Long Depression (1873-1896)
teaser: The first great depression of the industrial age followed the Panic of 1873, bringing deflation, strikes, and mass unemployment across Europe and America. It lasted over two decades, punctuated by booms and crashes. The era's hardships fueled both socialism and the scramble for protected markets and colonies.
byline: The industrial economies of the West

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the boom of the 1870s collapsed and why the depression lasted so long, then trace its political consequences.

name: Queen Zenobia (c. 240-274 CE)
teaser: After her husband's murder, Zenobia ruled the Palmyrene Empire, conquering Egypt and much of the Roman East and claiming descent from Cleopatra. She was defeated by the emperor Aurelian, paraded in Rome in golden chains, and then — according to most accounts — retired to a villa. Her brief empire was the last great challenge to Roman Syria.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Zenobia built her empire in Rome's crisis years, then trace her fall and the fate of Palmyra.

name: Mansa Musa (c. 1280-1337)
teaser: The emperor of Mali made the hajj to Mecca in 1324 with a caravan of thousands and so much gold that he crashed the metal's value in Cairo for a decade. His pilgrimage made Mali legendary and put West Africa on the world's maps. He built universities and mosques, and Timbuktu's golden age followed.

exploreAction.targetName: the reign and pilgrimage of Mansa Musa
exploreAction.instruction: Read how the pilgrimage's display of wealth remade Mali's reputation, then trace the scholarship the empire's gold funded.

name: Süleyman's Architect: Mimar Sinan (c. 1489-1588)
teaser: The chief architect of the Ottoman Empire for fifty years, Sinan built over 300 structures, including the Süleymaniye Mosque and the Selimiye at Edirne, which he called his masterpiece. His domes and minarets defined the skyline of the Ottoman world. He was a Christian boy conscripted into Ottoman service — and became the empire's greatest builder.
