The rival factions — the Blues and the Greens — were political forces in their own right, and their rivalry once ignited the Nika riots that nearly toppled Justinian. The circus's racing culture outlived the empire.
byline: The emperors and the racing factions of Rome

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the races and the factions worked, then trace the circus's role in the Nika riots and Roman political life.

name: The School of Athens (1511)
teaser: Raphael's fresco in the Vatican brings the philosophers of antiquity into one imagined hall — Plato pointing up, Aristotle gesturing to the world, Diogenes sprawled on the steps. The painting celebrates the marriage of philosophy and science that defined the Renaissance. Its figures are portraits of the era's greatest minds, including Leonardo as Plato and Raphael himself as Apelles.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the fresco organizes the history of philosophy, then trace the portraits and the symbolism of its architecture.

name: The Florentine Codex (1577)
teaser: Franciscan friar Bernardino de Sahagún spent decades interviewing Aztec elders and recording their knowledge — history, religion, medicine, and daily life — in Nahuatl with Spanish glosses. The twelve books of the Florentine Codex are the richest surviving record of Aztec civilization. Sahagún called it 'the work of those who know' — a native encyclopedia preserved by a colonial hand.
byline: Bernardino de Sahagún and his Nahua informants

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the interviews were conducted and organized, then consider what the codex preserves that the conquest destroyed.

name: The Good Neighbor Policy (1933-1940s)
teaser: FDR renounced military intervention in Latin America — the Good Neighbor Policy — replacing the gunboat diplomacy of the Roosevelt Corollary with cultural and economic engagement. The policy won goodwill during World War II, when Latin America's raw materials and bases mattered. The Cold War's interventions would betray its promise.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the policy changed U.S. relations with Latin America, then trace its limits during the Cold War.

name: The Sandinista Revolution (1979)
teaser: The Sandinista Front, named for the rebel Augusto Sandino, toppled the Somoza dictatorship in Nicaragua after years of guerrilla war — and then faced a U.S.-backed counterrevolution, the Contras. The civil war killed tens of thousands and turned Nicaragua into a Cold War battlefield. The Sandinistas returned to power democratically in 2006, now ruling as an increasingly authoritarian party.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the insurrection succeeded and the Contra war unfolded, then trace the Sandinistas' long return to power.

name: The Pinochet Regime (1973-1990)
teaser: After the 1973 coup, Augusto Pinochet ruled Chile for seventeen years, dismantling democracy and imposing a brutal military regime that tortured thousands and 'disappeared' over 3,000 people. His economic reforms — the 'Chicago Boys'' free-market experiment — made Chile a model for neoliberalism even as political freedom vanished. He was arrested in London in 1998, and his extradition fight became a landmark of international justice.
byline: Augusto Pinochet and the Chilean military

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the dictatorship governed and repressed, then trace the economic reforms and the long legal reckoning.

name: The NAFTA Agreement (1994)
teaser: The North American Free Trade Agreement eliminated most tariffs between the United States, Canada, and Mexico, creating the world's largest free-trade zone. Its supporters promised prosperity; its critics blamed it for offshoring jobs and hurting farmers. Replaced by the USMCA in 2020, NAFTA's legacy — the integration of North American manufacturing — remains hotly debated.
byline: The United States, Canada, and Mexico

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the agreement was negotiated and its effects measured, then trace its replacement by the USMCA.

name: The First Image of Earth from Space (1946)
teaser: A camera strapped to a captured German V-2 rocket, launched from New Mexico, returned the first photograph of Earth seen from space — a grainy shot from 65 miles up, showing clouds over the curvature of the planet. The image began the view-from-above that transformed science and imagination. Within a decade, satellites would map the whole globe.

exploreAction.targetName: the first photograph of Earth from space
exploreAction.instruction: Read how the V-2 film was recovered and developed, then trace the road from that first frame to the Blue Marble.
